teaser: A shy princess, a cascade of blue satin, and a portrait her husband hid behind a curtain.
review_notes:
Image matches the Met painting (signature and Broglie arms visible).
Commissioned 1851, finished 1853; Ingres was 72 at completion (lesson says 'in his seventies').
Nude study from a professional model for the pose: recalled from the Met's catalogue entry, please confirm.
Pendant described as in the style of ancient Roman jewelry (a 'bulla'): please confirm.
Pauline died of tuberculosis in 1860 at 35 (born 1825; 34 or 35 depending on the month).
Husband keeping the portrait behind a curtain: widely repeated, worded as 'is said'.
Sold 1958 to Robert Lehman; at the Met with the Lehman Collection since 1975.
Ingres vowing to stop painting portraits: paraphrase of repeated complaints in his letters, not a quote.

lesson.text: Where does your eye go first: to her face, or to her dress? Be honest. For most people the answer is that shimmering blue. Ingres knew it would be, and the tug of war between a quiet face and a spectacular gown is what this portrait is about.

She is Pauline, Princesse de Broglie. Her husband Albert, a young aristocrat who would one day head the French government, ordered the portrait in 1851. She was in her mid-twenties, a mother, very devout, and by all accounts painfully shy. Sitting still under a painter's stare was an ordeal for her.

Ingres, by then in his seventies, grumbled about portraits for most of his life. He saw himself as a painter of history and myth, and likenesses of society ladies as chores that stole his time. They are now his best-loved works.
He complained, and then he worked on this one for two years. The proof is in the materials. Satin, lace, gold, pearls: each is a separate problem in paint, and he solved them one at a time.

lesson.title: Four surfaces
lesson.text: Move from the widest area to the smallest.

spots.title: Satin
spots.text: The skirt is satin, a silk woven to be glossy. Ingres gives it hard white highlights on the ridges and deep blue in the hollows. No brushstroke shows: the paint is as smooth as the cloth.

spots.title: Lace
spots.text: On the sleeve, sheer white lace lies over the blue. He paints its flower pattern thread by thread and lets the color underneath show through the gaps.

spots.title: Wrists
spots.text: One arm carries a gold bracelet set with red stones, the other several strands of small pearls. Lower down, a ring glints on the hand that hangs in front of the skirt.

spots.title: The pendant
spots.text: A round gold pendant on a fine chain, in the style of ancient Roman jewelry, which was fashionable in the 1850s. It is the only ornament near her face.

lesson.text: All this shine does more than display wealth. Go back up to the face. It is pale, oval, perfectly even, with heavy eyelids and a gaze that is hard to read. Surrounded by so much glitter, her stillness comes across as reserve. The dress speaks so that she does not have to.

Ingres bent reality to get there. Her arms show no bones and barely an elbow; they curve like the handles of a vase. Her neck is long and her shoulders slope more than shoulders do. He had worked this way all his life: when the truth and a beautiful outline disagreed, the outline won.
To settle the pose, Ingres made preparatory drawings, including one of a nude studio model standing in for the princess. He often built his clothed portraits this way, from the body outward.
She is not dressed for a quiet afternoon. This is an evening gown, and the picture holds clues about the evening. They are piled on the yellow armchair she leans against.
She is about to go out, or has just come home. Can you find her gloves?

spots.title: Gloves and fan
spots.text: White gloves lie on the chair with a closed fan tucked just above them, a pale embroidered shawl and a dark wrap. A ball or the opera, perhaps. The portrait catches her between two rooms.

lesson.text: Two more things sit on the gray wall: Ingres's signature with the date 1853, at the left, about halfway up, and the Broglie family coat of arms in the upper right corner. Friends who saw the canvas in his studio admired it at once. Ingres swore, as he often did, that he was finished with portraits. He was not.
In an Ingres portrait, clothes are not decoration around the person. They carry the character: here, a blaze of satin that makes a shy woman's silence visible.

The story ends early. Pauline fell ill with tuberculosis, a lung disease with no cure at the time, and died in 1860, at 35. Albert never remarried. He is said to have kept the portrait behind a curtain for the rest of his life, and he lived another forty years. It left the family only in 1958, bought by the New York banker Robert Lehman, whose collection went to the Metropolitan Museum.
Knowing that, return to the first question. The satin is as loud as ever. Is it still the dress your eye goes to?

quiz.question: Who commissioned the portrait?
quiz.explanation: Albert ordered it in 1851, a few years into their marriage.

quiz.question: How did Ingres feel about painting portraits?
options: He considered them chores next to history painting
He refused to paint any after 1830
quiz.explanation: He grumbled that portraits stole time from grander subjects.

quiz.question: How does Ingres paint the blue satin?
options: Smoothly, with sharp white highlights and no visible strokes
quiz.explanation: The paint surface is as polished as the fabric it imitates.

quiz.question: What lies on the yellow armchair?
options: Gloves, a fan, a shawl and a wrap
quiz.explanation: The evening accessories suggest she is going out or has just returned.

quiz.question: What did her husband reportedly do with the portrait after her death?
quiz.explanation: He is said to have kept it covered for the rest of his life.

facts.text: The princess's arms are painted with careful anatomical accuracy.
facts.explanation: Ingres made them boneless curves, choosing a beautiful outline over the truth.

facts.text: Pauline de Broglie died in her mid-thirties of tuberculosis.
facts.explanation: She died in 1860, seven years after the portrait was finished.

facts.text: The portrait stayed in the Broglie family until the 1950s.
facts.explanation: It was sold in 1958 to the banker Robert Lehman.
